Below I walk through what’s needed, give an end‑to‑end workflow, and illustrate how you could run this in Python—using either simple Linear Regression or a more flexible Random Forest Regressor. --- ### 1️⃣ What You Need First | Item | Why It Matters | |------|----------------| | Historical monthly/quarterly observations of:
• Median / average house price
• Interest rate (e.g., Fed funds rate)
• Unemployment rate | These will form your training data. | | A clear target horizon – “next 5 years” means 60 months ahead (if monthly). | Determines how far out you forecast. | If you already have a CSV file (`housing_data.csv`) containing columns `date`, `price`, `int_rate`, `unemp` you’re ready to jump into modeling. If not, let me know what format your data lives in so I can help you load it! --- ### 2️⃣ Quick Data Prep Checklist ```python import pandas as pd from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split ``` * Load & parse dates → `pd.read_csv(..., parse_dates=['date'])` * Sort chronologically * Create lagged features if desired (e.g., previous month’s price) * Split into *train* vs *future* periods: ```python X_train = df[['int_rate', 'unemp']].iloc[:-60] # all except last 5 yrs y_train = df['price'].iloc[:-60] X_future = df[['int_rate', 'unemp']].tail(60) # last 5 yr period ``` --- ### 3️⃣ Modeling Options #### Option A – Simple Linear Regression Good baseline when relationships appear roughly linear. ```python from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression model_lr = LinearRegression() model_lr.fit(X_train, y_train) preds_5yr = model_lr.predict(X_future) print(preds_5yr.head()) ``` #### Option B – Random Forest Regressor Captures non‑linear interactions without heavy feature engineering. ```python from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, random_state=42) rf.fit(X_train, y_train) preds_rf = rf.predict(X_future) print(preds_rf[:12]) # first year ``` Both models output point forecasts for each month in the next 5 years.
